parts.article:
Lawrence Johnston and Hidcote Garden V2

(A) Today, the National Trust in the UK administers hundreds of public gardens, but sixty-odd years ago there was only one: Hidcote Manor near the English village of Chipping Campden. In 1949, Hidcote attracted a mere 600 visitors and took only £30 during its first public season. Nowadays, Hidcote is famous worldwide as a masterpiece of design and planting, attracting 150,000 visitors and raising nearly £1 million annually from entrance tickets.

(B) Hidcote Garden was the creation of an American in Britain, the shy Major Lawrence Johnston, who came to live on the site in 1907 with his widowed mother, Gertrude Winthrop. In some respects, Winthrop feared her son's talents for expensive landscape gardening and never allowed him full access to the family's funds. Nonetheless, with her inspiration and guidance, Johnston started his design in 1908 and brought it to a peak in the early 1930s when he was in his 60s. At that time, Johnston may rightly be ranked beside Harold Nicolson and Vita Sackville-West, creators of Sissinghurst, his garden's only surviving equal.

(C) In the last years of his life, Johnston placed faith in his head gardener Nancy Lindsay. Lindsay was undoubtedly a skilled plantswoman, but she had many other talents as well, including one for taking offence. Johnston was ill-suited to dealing with her impassioned views. When the National Trust subsequently acquired the garden from Johnston, none of his crucial garden diaries could be found, and some speculated that Lindsay had burned them to hurt her employer. Whatever their actual fate, Trust gardener Graham Thomas was tasked with reviving Hidcote. Without these crucial documents, Thomas had to rely on his instincts. He knew that for the gardens to be a commercial success, he needed to extend areas of most interest to the general public, so he introduced new plants and a Mediterranean Bank where Johnston had planted nothing of the sort, while retaining the superb structure of avenues and evergreen rooms. As a result, since 1949, the visiting public has innocently been admiring Thomas's flower plantings, not Johnston's own. When the important designer Russell Page visited Hidcote in 1934, he hailed the half-hardy plants in the summer house as one of the highlights. However, Thomas later removed these plants and pulled the house down, fearing that such relatively colourless exhibits would not capture the public's imagination.

(D) Then, in 2002, Johnston's old diaries and notebooks resurfaced. The present head gardener had started giving lectures about Hidcote's lost early designs, during which he appealed for memories from his audience. A few months later, an envelope arrived. There was no letter inside, only Johnston's personal diaries from the 1920s and 30s. The sender remains unknown, but the importance of these documents to Hidcote is certain. They contain invaluable notes regarding the selection of plants and, even better still, detailed sketches by Johnston himself showing how the different parts of the garden are related and how those relationships evolve over the seasons. These documents are a rarity in other ways too, for they never dwell on the issues typically addressed in diaries—relationships, loves, and longings. These are far more interesting, as they represent a classic social history of an English country house during the inter-war years.

(E) On page after page, Johnston describes the layout of the plants and gardens, interspersed with notes about that day's guests. The famous novelist Edith Wharton is recorded as coming for lunch, beside a recipe for poison to kill garden weeds. It is this mix of glamour and the everyday that makes the diaries so fascinating. At their heart, though, these are useful documents containing, for example, lengthy lists of those who might one day be of service around the estate, including local stonemasons and glaziers, or repairers of broken china from as far away as France.

(F) The discovery of the diaries has offered Hidcote a new direction for the years ahead. Inspired by them, an anonymous American has donated £1.6 million to the gardens. This remarkable chance has been seized by the Trust to fund crucial repair work on paths and the famous pool, as well as the reconstruction of the old summer house. However, the real implications of the discoveries made from the diaries are more challenging, as the Trust now possesses information about the very plants that most appealed to Johnston during the garden's golden years. Today, these may not be easy to source or appealing to contemporary tastes.

(G) ‘But isn’t it all so long ago?’ a non-gardening academic recently asked me. On the contrary, Hidcote is still with us, a living legacy. It includes the greatest central vista in British gardening, a design I regard as the greatest in British art in the past century. It was the work of an American genius building an un-American garden of his own. I do not believe the fashionable guess that Johnston was informed by books on contemporary design by Britain’s Thomas Mawson, an altogether less innovative mind. This is because so much in the garden reminds us how Johnston had travelled widely in Europe, which Mawson had not. Johnston’s own origins, the events of his life, and his individual design flair all contribute to making Hidcote so unique.

analyses.content: 原文提到首席园丁做了关于花园“早期遗失设计”的讲座后，收到了匿名寄来的日记，这对应了选项中的“初始计划”。
只要定位到讲座的主题是关于“设计”并进行同义替换，即可排除其他无关选项。

"The present head gardener had started giving lectures about Hidcote's lost early designs, during which he appealed for memories from his audience. A few months later, an envelope arrived. There was no letter inside, only Johnston's personal diaries from the 1920s and 30s."
原文说更棒的是Johnston本人画的“详细草图”展示了花园随季节的变化，直接对应选项中的“图画”。
你可能想选B，但原文明确指出展示季节变化的是他亲手画的草图，而不是植物本身。

"They contain invaluable notes regarding the selection of plants and, even better still, detailed sketches by Johnston himself showing how the different parts of the garden are related and how those relationships evolve over the seasons."
原文指出这些日记从不记录感情、爱与渴望这些常规话题，说明我们很难从中了解到他的“私生活”。
你可能试图从前文找答案，但破解此题的关键在于一定要关注并理解原文中“从不提及”这个否定表达。
"These documents are a rarity in other ways too, for they never dwell on the issues typically addressed in diaries—relationships, loves, and longings."
原文提到日记里记录了当天的“客人”，比如著名小说家来吃午餐，这直接对应了选项中的知名“访客”。
只要准确找到原文中的客人（guests）并识别出它是选项中访客（visitors）的同义词，就不会选错。

"On page after page, Johnston describes the layout of the plants and gardens, interspersed with notes about that day's guests. The famous novelist Edith Wharton is recorded as coming for lunch, beside a recipe for poison to kill garden weeds."
原文列举了远至法国的石匠、玻璃匠以及修补瓷器的人，这些靠手艺干活的职业统称为“手工艺人”。
你可能不认识石匠和玻璃匠，但通过后面补充的“修补破碎瓷器的人”也能准确猜出这是一类手工业者。

"At their heart, though, these are useful documents containing, for example, lengthy lists of those who might one day be of service around the estate, including local stonemasons and glaziers, or repairers of broken china from as far away as France."

questions.question: Gardening may be considered a form of art.

analyses.content: 作者明确表示自己将花园中央景观视为上个世纪英国“最伟大的艺术”，这证明了园艺可以被视为一种艺术形式。
你可能觉得题目说法太主观，但作者在这里正是使用了明确的个人评价来肯定这一观点。
"It includes the greatest central vista in British gardening, a design I regard as the greatest in British art in the past century."

questions.question: The original design of Hidcote should be retained as closely as possible.

analyses.content: 原文只提到了解最初的植物种类带来了挑战，因为它们可能难找且不符合现代口味，但作者并没有表态“是否应该尽可能保留原始设计”。
你可能看到了信托基金在做重建和修复工作，就自己脑补作者支持完全复原，但这纯属过度推断，原文根本没提。

"However, the real implications of the discoveries made from the diaries are more challenging, as the Trust now possesses information about the very plants that most appealed to Johnston during the garden's golden years. Today, these may not be easy to source or appealing to contemporary tastes."

questions.question: Mawson was the most significant influence on Johnston's work.

analyses.content: 作者直白地说“我不相信”Johnston受到了Mawson的影响，并贬低Mawson缺乏创新，这完全否定了题目中的说法。
你可能只看到了Mawson的名字出现在原文中，却没注意到紧挨在前面的“我不相信”这一核心否定判断。

"I do not believe the fashionable guess that Johnston was informed by books on contemporary design by Britain’s Thomas Mawson, an altogether less innovative mind. This is because so much in the garden reminds us how Johnston had travelled widely in Europe, which Mawson had not."

questions.question: Hidcote reflects aspects of Johnston's life experience.

analyses.content: 原文总结道，Johnston的出身、他生活中的事件（也就是生活经历）以及个人才华，共同造就了Hidcote的独特性，这与题目说法完美契合。
你可能想在原文中找生活经历的原词，但原文的“他生活中的事件”和“在欧洲广泛旅行”就是对他生活经历的具体表达。

"This is because so much in the garden reminds us how Johnston had travelled widely in Europe, which Mawson had not. Johnston’s own origins, the events of his life, and his individual design flair all contribute to making Hidcote so unique."
